[0] everyday_reading (E): In everyday life '7' and 7 are the same thing, and a character is a letter, not a number. A Java char is a 16-bit numeric code: '7' has code 55, and 'a' + 1 is the int 98.
[1] misconception (M) -> CharNotNumeric: wrong rule: char is not a numeric type. Right rule: A char is encoded as a 16-bit integer, so arithmetic such as 'b' + 'c' or 'a' + 4 works on the character codes.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> CharNotNumeric: Points to LT (a char in arithmetic becomes its int code). Applied unevenly, a student treats 'b' + 'c' as 197 in one exercise but prints it as "bc" in another. (here mixing in: "char is not a numeric type")

[0] names_the_element (N): char: the primitive type for a single 16-bit Unicode character, such as 'a', '%' or '\n'.
[1] states_the_rule (S): A char literal is exactly one character (or one escape sequence) in single quotes. Values range from '\u0000' to '\uffff' (0 to 65535), and char is an integral type. A char literal is one character in single quotes ('a'); a String literal is any sequence in double quotes ("a"), so 'a' and "a" have different types and 'ab' does not compile.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): When a char meets an arithmetic operator, it is first promoted to int (its code) and the operation runs in int. Storing the result back in a char needs an explicit cast.
[1] output_prediction (OP): System.out.println('b') prints b. 'b' + 'c' is the int 197. (char) ('a' + 4) is 'e'.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): c++ on char c = 'A' makes c 'B', because increment works on chars directly. c = c + 1; does not compile, because the right side is an int.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): A char is stored as an unsigned 16-bit code, so in arithmetic it acts as an int ('a' + 1 is 98). Going from int to char needs a cast.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A char widens automatically to double (its code), but a double needs a cast to become a char. A char never holds a fractional part.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): char and boolean are unrelated: there is no conversion or cast between them, and 'c' is never true or false.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): Char arithmetic works on each char's numeric code and yields an int. A cast turns the result back into a character.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): char is one of the eight primitive types: the unsigned 16-bit integral one, used for single characters.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): 'a' is a char (one 16-bit character code, a primitive); "a" is a String (a sequence of characters, an object). 'a' + 'b' is the int 195, while "a" + "b" is "ab".
[6] purpose_of_the_whole (P): A char holds one character: processing text one character at a time (charAt), looping over 'A'..'Z', or shifting letters in a cipher.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> CharNotNumeric: Changing 'A' to "A" changes the type to String, so + concatenates instead of adding. Changing a char variable to int keeps the arithmetic, but println then prints numbers instead of letters.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use char for one character from a literal or from charAt, especially when the character's code matters (alphabet loops, ciphers). Use String for text of any length.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A char literal holds exactly one character. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Several characters in single quotes ('ab') or a word in single quotes: 'unclosed character literal'.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: int arithmetic on chars yields an int, which cannot go into a char without a cast. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: char c = 'a' + i; or c = c + 1; with variable i: 'possible lossy conversion from int to char'.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A char compares by its code, not by the digit or letter it shows. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Comparing a char with an int as if it were a digit (seat <= 3 for seat = 'A'), or printing c + 1 expecting a letter.
wrong: A char is only a letter, so c + k is an error. | right: A char is encoded as a 16-bit integer, so arithmetic such as 'b' + 'c' or 'a' + 4 works on the character codes.
wrong: char is not a numeric type | right: A char is encoded as a 16-bit integer, so arithmetic such as 'b' + 'c' or 'a' + 4 works on the character codes.
A boolean holds true or false; a char holds a single character such as 'c'.
'a' is a char (one 16-bit character code, a primitive); "a" is a String (a sequence of characters, an object). 'a' + 'b' is the int 195, while "a" + "b" is "ab".
A double holds a number with a fractional part; a char holds one character code, which is a whole number.
An int holds a whole number; a char holds one character, which Java stores as its numeric code.
Char arithmetic uses the numeric code stored for each char.
char is one of the eight primitive types, the one used for single characters.
